title: Drug safety testing, disposals and dealing in an English field: Exploring the operational and behavioural outcomes of the UK’s first onsite ‘drug checking’ service

claims.statement: In people who use drugs given test strips or colour test kits to check their own drugs, handing out kits compared with not handing them out: the evidence is insufficient to say whether it causes harm, for example through false reassurance after a negative result, or reduces harm, and the question is disputed. No study read compared people given kits with people not given them on harm or overdose. What was measured shows few riskier responses: in a British Columbia take-home programme, 6 of 336 survey answers (2 in 100) described using alone or using more or faster after a strip showed fentanyl, in answer to standard questions, and the one study comparing overdoses in people who did and did not use strips found no clear difference, in an imprecise estimate (risk ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.70 to 2.06). But no study read reports what people did after a negative result (the take-home programme asked and did not report it); a scoping review relays people believing that a negative strip means xylazine or that a darker line means stronger fentanyl, one person saying a negative result would mean using a little more, and strips missing carfentanil and other drugs; and at home, strips showed fentanyl in 73 of 265 methamphetamine samples (28 in 100) and 16 of 93 cocaine samples (17 in 100), against 5 of 97 (5 in 100) and 1 of 92 (1 in 100) tested by staff on site, which the authors think more likely reflects how the tests were done than a different supply. Two critiques argue, without data, that frequent positive results without ill effects could breed complacency, that people who want fentanyl may seek a positive result, and that a colour test showing MDMA may be read as meaning a pill is safe; one of them still supports handing out strips with guidance and naloxone. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Klaire: riskier responses 6/336 answers (1.8%; Wilson 0.8–3.8%, editors' calculation), 1 using more or faster and 5 using alone; responses to a negative result asked but not reported; take-home against on-site positivity, crystal methamphetamine 73/265 (27.6%) against 5/97 (5.2%), difference 22.4 points (14.8–30.1), cocaine 16/93 (17.2%) against 1/92 (1.1%), 16.1 (7.1–25.1). Vickers-Smith: nonfatal overdose adjusted RR 1.20 (0.70–2.06), unadjusted 2.06 (1.09–3.89); composite risk-reduction score 0.86 points higher (0.34–1.38) on 0–15. Kutscher (relayed): riskier use in two studies; difficulty interpreting results 3% to almost 34%. No study reports behaviour after a negative result.

claims.statement: In people who had drugs tested at an English festival (2016) or with fentanyl test strips in North America (2016 to 2019), a result showing something unexpected, compared with an expected result, is associated with more people getting rid of drugs, though most did not, and how many depended on the setting. At one English festival, where chemists tested drugs on site and staff gave each result in a consultation, 30 of 45 people whose drug was not what it had been sold as (67 in 100) handed over drugs for police destruction, against 15 of 164 whose drug matched (9 in 100); the service saw these handovers, but people may have kept or thrown away other drugs elsewhere, and 111 of the 164 with a matching result said they would take their usual amount. Among people who use opioids, few said they got rid of a drug after a strip showed fentanyl: at a Vancouver supervised injection site, staff recorded an intention to throw the drug away after 50 of 436 checks before use that showed fentanyl (11 in 100), against 10 of 134 that did not (7 in 100), a difference that may be chance (odds ratio 1.60, 95% CI 0.79 to 3.26), and in a Rhode Island pilot 10 in 100 of 31 young adults with a positive strip said they threw the drugs out. A systematic review of drug checking services to 2019 reports disposal from 0 to 10 in 100 across studies, observed at Canadian festivals at 4 and 7 in 100, and more often after unexpected results; the authors of the Vancouver study link the low rate to dependence, lack of money to replace drugs and no access to unadulterated drugs. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Festival (observed): 30/45 (66.7%; Wilson 52.1–78.6%) against 15/164 (9.1%; 5.6–14.5%), p < .01; difference 57.5 points (Newcombe 42.0–70.0), risk ratio 7.3 (editors' calculations); 49/230 (21.3%) overall; stated intention to take the usual amount 111/164 (67.7%) with a matching result against 4/45 (8.9%) with a non-matching one. Vancouver (stated, before use): 50/436 (11.5%) against 10/134 (7.5%), OR 1.60 (0.79–3.26); risk difference 4.0 points (−2.3 to 8.7, editors' calculation). Rhode Island (self-report, n = 31): threw out 10%, sold 10%, gave away 7%. Review (relayed): 0–10% across studies; observed 4% (n = 2078) and 7% (n = 2786) at Canadian festivals.

claims.statement: At one 25,000-capacity festival in England, the first year with an on-site drug checking service (2016, when chemists analysed 247 samples and staff gave results in 230 consultations, with alerts to on-site agencies), compared with the year before (2015): the evidence is insufficient to say whether the service changed drug-related hospital admissions. The festival's figures, from unpublished police reports, were 19 drug-related admissions among 59 admissions in 2015 and 1 among 50 in 2016; admissions not classed as drug-related rose from 40 to 49 (editors' calculation), paramedics were said to have treated more people on site rather than sending them to hospital, the agencies and indicators behind the records changed between years, and the author states that the pilot cannot show what part the service played. This was testing by chemists at one festival, with one year before and one after and no comparison festival; it says nothing about kits used at home. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Drug-related admissions 19 of 59 in 2015 against 1 of 50 in 2016 (a 95% fall as printed); admissions not classed as drug-related 40 then 49 (editors' calculation). No interval or test. No drug-related deaths at the festival in 2016, a year with six at UK festivals; the author notes that deaths at festivals are rare and often have several causes.
